findings.title: Equal-order providers are now picked silently instead of failing
findings.body: Detection used to throw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by `order()` and silently takes the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so the sort is stable and ties fall back to ServiceLoader/classpath order. The only notice is a debug log. If a FIPS deployment accidentally ships both the FIPS and default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) providers, it can now quietly run on the non-FIPS provider. The old fail-fast guard should be kept for ties at the highest order, or the FIPS provider should be given a distinct higher order.

findings.title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI. Any third-party or downstream implementation (custom crypto providers, the separate keycloak-client repository) will no longer compile. Already-compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when `detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order`. Declaring it as a `default` method returning a baseline value would keep compatibility.

findings.title: Test uses one default-curve key for every algorithm and only checks self round-trip
findings.body: A single key from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` (JDK default curve: P-256 or P-384 depending on JDK version) is reused for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The test only asserts that DER→RS→DER→RS gives the same result as the first RS conversion. Because `integerToBytes` truncates or pads, a lossy conversion still passes: on a JDK whose default is P-384, ES256 truncates r/s to 32 bytes and both sides match. The test never checks that a converted DER signature still verifies with `Signature.verify`, never uses the curve that matches each algorithm, and never compares output against the BC-based provider. Encoding bugs would go undetected.

findings.title: integerToBytes silently truncates values longer than the expected length
findings.body: When `bytes.length > qLength`, the high-order bytes are dropped without any check. This is correct only when the extra byte is the 0x00 sign byte. For a malformed or mismatched-curve signature where r or s really exceeds `signLength/2` bytes, the method returns a corrupted value instead of throwing an IOException. That produces wrong JWS signatures or misleading verification results. It should reject the value when the dropped bytes are non-zero.

findings.title: Dead code: ASN1 encoders created and discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 build ASN1Encoder instances for r and s and throw the results away. The same encoding is done again in the return statement. This is leftover code that wastes allocations and should be removed.
